title: Argentum Health - streaming latency, fanout & hosting path discovery
summary: Intro discovery focused on p95 streaming latency targets, concurrency shape, and whether hosted/dedicated/private fits Argentum's regulatory and burst fanout needs. Agreed to run a token/sec + streaming p95 benchmark with a 3-config matrix and share security package.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
action_items: Maya: Send benchmark template + example load profile (by 2027-11-25)
Liam: Spin up a quick Redwood hosted micro-benchmark with 10/50/200 concurrency profiles and share results (by 2027-11-30)
Eli: Provide sample request/response size distribution and expected avg tokens per request (by 2027-11-24)
Hannah: Confirm data residency / KMS requirements and share security contact (by 2027-11-26)
next_steps: Run three benches (hosted fast path, dedicated reserved pool, private VPC lite) and compare p95 token latency and token/sec cost
Redwood to send security pack (SOC2, ISO, network design, KMS integration doc)
Schedule hands-on pilot kickoff if bench results meet p95 < 300ms target for streaming token latency
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-11-23
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 36 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam O'Connor, Priya Rao (Redwood) / Raj Patel, Sofia Morales, Eli Turner, Hannah Liu (Argentum)

Summary (auto): quick discovery to nail p95 streaming SLAs and decide hosting path. Some audio dropouts mid-call.

Topics: p95 target, concurrency/burst fanout, hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs, security and KMS, benchmarking plan

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:05] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Liam and Priya from the infra team. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Raj Patel: Good, thanks. On our side it's Raj, CTO, so we'll jump in. Sofia and Eli are on for the technical bits, Hannah on security.
[00:00:20] Maya Chen: Awesome. High level, you've flagged streaming p95 and burst fanout as the gating criteria, so want to get into the shapes and constraints. Sofia, do you want to kick off with what you're seeing in prod today?
[00:00:32] Sofia Morales: Yeah sure. So, we run a conversational triage assistant for inbound patient messages. Typical request ~60-120 tokens incoming, model generates 150-600 tokens. Peak events are like appointment windows where thousands of small requests hit in bursts. Our target is p95 per-token latency under 300 milliseconds in streaming mode, and we need the system to handle concurrency spikes up to ~2k concurrent streams for 30-90s without failing.
[00:00:58] Liam O'Connor: Okay that's helpful. When you say 2k concurrent streams, is that long-lived streaming connections, or short lived?
[00:01:06] Sofia Morales: They're websocket-ish streams that stay open for the entire generation. Most lasts under 12 seconds, but during peak campaigns, half the requests start within a small window, so it's a fanout problem.
[00:01:18] Priya Rao: Got it. And do you have a strict SLO on end-to-end request completion or you're breaking it down to per-token p95 on the streaming frames?
[00:01:26] Raj Patel: We'll accept some tail on total completion, but the UX depends on the streaming frames arriving quickly. So token-level p95 is the primary measure. If token frames are slow, users see stalls.
[00:01:36] Maya Chen: Perfect. That maps to how we think about streaming SLOs — continuous batching and KV cache behavior are big drivers. Quick question: are you currently self-hosting any models or using an API?
[00:01:48] Eli Turner: Right now it's a mix. We call an external hosted provider for model inference right now but have some on-prem experiments for sensitive flows. Latency's okay at baseline but tails during bursts are the issue.
[00:01:58] Liam O'Connor: Makes sense. So we should look at three paths: Redwood Hosted (fastest to run a bench and low friction), Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool with predictable throughput), and Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem for strict residency). Each has predictable differences in routing and isolation that affect tail latencies.
[00:02:15] Raj Patel: Yep. For compliance we may need Private for certain workflows, but we'd like to keep critical real-time triage on Hosted or Dedicated if they hit p95.
[00:02:24] [00:02:30] Hannah Liu: Quick Q on encryption — we use a customer-managed KMS and need to ensure keys never leave our control. Is that supported?
[00:02:36] Maya Chen: Yes — Private supports customer KMS/HSM integration, Dedicated can be configured to meet that for enterprise tiers, and Hosted can meet encryption at rest but for customer-managed keys we usually recommend Dedicated or Private. We'll send the detailed KMS integration doc.
[00:02:48] [00:03:05] Sofia Morales: Also curious about prefix/KV cache invalidation. Our prompts often share a 1–2 sentence context that could be cached. How aggressive is your prefix caching and does that change token/sec?
[00:03:15] Liam O'Connor: Great question. Our runtime does automatic prefix/KV caching keyed by request fingerprint. In streaming, cached KV can avoid recomputing early layers which reduces per-token compute by up to ~40% in our internal tests, but cache hit rate depends on request similarity. We'll need a sample workload to estimate hit rate.
[00:03:33] Maya Chen: And caching interacts with quantization and batching as well — when you use an int8 quant profile we'll show different kernel paths.
[00:03:41] Raj Patel: For benchmarks we can provide a request sample. Eli will push the traffic shape and request sizes after the call.
[00:03:48] Eli Turner: Yep I'll send a CSV with timestamps, tokens in, tokens out, and a simple distribution.
[00:03:54] [00:04:10] Priya Rao: On the benchmarking side, we usually do a matrix: small concurrency (10), mid (50-100), and high burst (200-2000) with realistic think times. For streaming p95 we instrument at the per-token emit time. Any objections to that approach?
[00:04:22] Sofia Morales: No that's fine. We also want to measure token/sec efficiency because cost matters; show us tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
[00:04:30] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely. We'll report p50/p95/p99 for per-token latency, tokens/sec, and token cost. For Dedicated we'll include reserved throughput numbers and burst elasticity.
[00:04:40] [00:05:05] Raj Patel: Two architecture constraints: we need <300ms p95 streaming frames for the triage use-case, and during burst windows the platform mustn't drop or queue connections excessively — graceful degradation preferred to failures. Can you outline what graceful fallback looks like?
[00:05:18] Maya Chen: Typically we do tiered fallbacks: route to a cheaper model variant for non-critical tokens, fall back to a smaller model for initial summary frames, or switch to a synchronous fast path with truncated completions. For Hosted, we implement policy routing; for Dedicated, you can pin model variants to the pool; for Private, you'd control the deployment.
[00:05:36] [00:05:50] Sofia Morales: If you route to a smaller model, how do you control quality regression? We can't have major drops for clinical phrasing.
[00:05:57] Liam O'Connor: Good point. We have eval tooling that runs prompt sets against model variants and flags regressions. In production you'd whitelist prompt families that can tolerate fallback. This is part of Redwood Optimize.
[00:06:10] [00:06:30] Hannah Liu: Regarding compliance: SOC2 is table stakes for us; also need audit logs of token-level requests and optional redaction. How does Redwood expose logs?
[00:06:38] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdowns with retention settings. For Private deployments you can push logs to your SIEM or use our S3-compatible export. We'll include audit log examples.
[00:06:49] [00:07:05] Raj Patel: Cool. Can we get a sense of numbers? If we target p95 < 300ms, what does that look like for, say, a 4k-token generation in streaming with 200 concurrent streams on Dedicated?
[00:07:18] Liam O'Connor: A 4k generation streaming out at 30–60 tokens/sec on average will span multiple seconds. But p95 per-token depends on burst contention and batching latency. In our internal gbench, on a reserved A100-like pool, with tuned batching, we can hold streaming token p95 in the 150–250ms range for models in the 7B-13B family at 100–200 concurrency. For 4k tokens and 200 concurrents it's borderline; you'd want Dedicated with higher reserved throughput or apply prefix caching to cut cost.
[00:07:48] Sofia Morales: We're mostly on a 13B family right now. That matches what you described.
[00:07:54] [00:08:20] Priya Rao: Important note — model architecture and sequence length drive kernel selection. Long sequences push memory and make continuous batching tricky, so sometimes we pick a model variant with better long-seq performance for heavy tails.
[00:08:32] Eli Turner: You mentioned kernel selection — do you expose metric of sequence-length distribution hits so we could tune?
[00:08:38] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Console shows sequence length histograms and per-model kernel path metrics. We'll share sample dashboards.
[00:08:47] [00:09:10] Raj Patel: On the Hosted vs Dedicated decision: cost is a factor, but predictability and our regulatory constraints push towards Dedicated. Can you explain how Dedicated handles burst beyond reserved capacity?
[00:09:22] Maya Chen: Dedicated has configurable autoscaling and a burst pool. Contracts define committed capacity and a burst tier for transient demand. For firm SLAs, you can combine Dedicated with a failover to Hosted as an overflow path if you accept sending data to a Hosted transit (we can anonymize payloads or use model variants).
[00:09:41] Hannah Liu: That overflow to Hosted is sensitive for us. We need to know data residency impacts and whether any PHI leaves our VPC.
[00:09:48] Maya Chen: Understood — if PHI is in scope, Private or on-prem is safer. Dedicated can be configured to keep data in-region and integrate with your KMS, but overflow to Hosted would typically be off for PHI. We'll document the behavior.
[00:10:00] [00:10:22] Sofia Morales: For the bench, can Redwood run a synchronous token emitter that simulates 2k websocket streams starting in a heavy fanout window? That shape is the key variable.
[00:10:33] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We can orchestrate a synthetic fanout driver with configurable start jitter and think time. We'll run it against the three modes. Maya: we'll need sample payloads and token distribution.
[00:10:44] Maya Chen: Noted. Eli will provide the CSV.
[00:10:48] Eli Turner: I'll send it after the call. Also, if we run bench on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, will the results be comparable? Network paths differ and might skew p95.
[00:10:58] Priya Rao: Good point. We'll normalize by reporting breakdowns: client-to-edge network, routing latency, and inference runtime. We'll also capture per-token server-side timestamps so you can see the server contribution to p95 separately.
[00:11:12] [00:11:40] Raj Patel: What about warm/cold start behavior? We have a lot of small models and don't want cold-start spikes during marketing campaigns.
[00:11:48] Liam O'Connor: For Dedicated you can keep warming pools or pinned cores to avoid cold starts. Our runtime supports pre-warming and model pinning. Hosted has slightly more variability on cold starts unless you buy sustained concurrency reservations.
[00:12:00] Sofia Morales: And how long does quantization tuning take? We might want int8 profiles to reduce token cost.
[00:12:08] Priya Rao: Quant tuning depends on model size and dataset. For a 13B model, we typically have a conservative int8 profile in days for a basic validation; production-quality quant plus evals might take 1–2 weeks. We'll propose default profiles and show expected latency and quality delta.
[00:12:22] [00:12:50] Raj Patel: For the fanout scenario: if we see 2k concurrent streams for a minute, what's the recommended approach to keep p95 low? More reserved GPUs, more autoscale, or architectural changes?
[00:13:02] Liam O'Connor: A hybrid: reserve enough base capacity in Dedicated for typical peaks, rely on burst pool for short spikes, and architect the app to have a short circuit for noncritical flows — for example, precompute templated replies or shard the workload by region to avoid global fanout. Also, use prefix caching aggressively.
[00:13:18] Sofia Morales: Sharding regionally is doable. We have multiple regions but prefer single-region for synced state. Can Redwood route by policy?
[00:13:26] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing lets you route by region, cost, or latency policies and do fallback by policy. We'll include a routing diagram.
[00:13:36] [00:14:00] Eli Turner: A practical ask: can you run a 3x scenario — low/mid/high — and show per-token p95 and cost per million tokens in a single sheet so we can do quick TCO math?
[00:14:11] Maya Chen: Yes, that's part of the bench deliverable. We'll include a short TCO calc and assumptions.
[00:14:18] [00:14:35] Hannah Liu: Are there any limits on connection counts per node in Hosted? We worry about connection fds at scale.
[00:14:42] Priya Rao: There are connection scaling strategies. Fronting proxies handle large numbers, but per-node limits exist; we shard across frontends and autoscale. We'll include scaling guidance for websocket-like connections.
[00:14:56] [00:15:20] Raj Patel: Can you share any real-world reference where p95 streaming < 300ms during spikes was achieved?
[00:15:28] Liam O'Connor: We ran a retail partner with flash sales where we achieved ~220ms p95 on Dedicated at 1500 concurrent streams for 10–40s bursts with a 13B model using prefix caching and pinned pools. We'll anonymize the deck and share the benchmark story.
[00:15:42] Sofia Morales: That sounds promising.
[00:15:48] [00:16:10] Maya Chen: I'll summarize the bench plan: Redwood runs three bench configs — Hosted baseline, Dedicated reserved pool with burst, and Private VPC-lite. Each runs 10/100/500/2000 concurrency profiles with fanout windows, measures per-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost. We'll add kernel path metrics and sequence-length histograms.
[00:16:29] Raj Patel: Timeline?
[00:16:32] Maya Chen: We can get Hosted bench back in 3 days after the workload is provided, Dedicated bench in ~1 week to schedule reserved capacity, Private depends on your on-prem/hybrid availability but we can do a small VPC-lite test in 10 days.
[00:16:44] Eli Turner: 3 days for Hosted is great. We'll prioritize that dataset.
[00:16:49] [00:17:15] Sofia Morales: A small accuracy note — we sometimes need deterministic tokens for downstream auditing; is there a way to get deterministic generation in streaming?
[00:17:25] Liam O'Connor: Determinism depends on sampling settings (temperature, seed) and model randomness. For near-deterministic behavior, set temperature zero and use a fixed seed; we can instrument that. But distributed batching can introduce ordering differences, so pinning a single inference lane helps.
[00:17:40] [00:18:05] Raj Patel: Any obvious blockers? For example, HIPAA or PHI requirements?
[00:18:12] Hannah Liu: PHI is in scope for the triage assistant. We'll probably push PHI flows to Private but want low-risk flows on Dedicated/Hosted. We need contract-level assurances for dedup logs and retention.
[00:18:24] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll include contract language examples and retention controls in the security pack.
[00:18:33] [00:18:55] Priya Rao: Practical misc note: when running bench against Hosted we instrument both client and server side; the server-side token timestamp is critical to separate network jitter.
[00:19:03] Sofia Morales: We'll want both.
[00:19:08] [00:19:40] Raj Patel: If the Hosted bench meets p95 < 300ms for our mid and high workloads, are there special pricing or contractual things we should be aware of before going prod?
[00:19:50] Maya Chen: If Hosted works, we can propose an SLA and volume discounts for committed usage. Dedicated requires a reservation contract; pricing is more predictable. We'll include ballpark numbers in the bench sheet.
[00:20:02] [00:20:30] Eli Turner: For data egress, we have multi-cloud attachment — will that affect latency reporting?
[00:20:38] Priya Rao: We'll record the egress path and show per-region differences. If you have mid-tier proxies, include them in the topology.
[00:20:48] [00:21:10] Raj Patel: Okay last questions from me: is there an option to do a canary traffic split across hosting modes to test in production?
[00:21:18] Maya Chen: Yes, we support traffic splits and rollouts with automatic fallback. You can route a small percentage to Dedicated or Private and ramp. Rollback is automatic on error thresholds.
[00:21:28] Sofia Morales: Good.
[00:21:40] [00:22:00] Maya Chen: Quick recap of next steps: Eli sends workload, Maya/Liam run Hosted bench in ~3 days, deliverables include p50/p95/p99 token latencies, tokens/sec, cost, kernel metrics, and a TCO sheet. Security pack goes to Hannah. Schedule follow-up pilot planning session after bench.
[00:22:18] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:22:24] [00:22:40] Hannah Liu: One small ask — include sample audit log entries and retention options.
[00:22:46] Maya Chen: Will do.
[00:23:00] [00:23:15] Sofia Morales: Also include a short note on expected regression if using int8 quant vs fp16 for our model family.
[00:23:22] Priya Rao: We'll include a quality delta estimate and suggested eval prompts.
[00:23:29] [00:23:50] Eli Turner: I'll send payloads and a short readme of the traffic shape within the hour.
[00:23:58] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with the bench template and a calendar invite for the next checkpoint.
[00:24:08] [00:24:30] -- audio glitch -- some words dropped -- reconnecting --
[00:24:55] [00:25:10] Raj Patel: Sorry about packet loss at our side, should be stable now.
[00:25:17] [00:25:40] Maya Chen: No worries. Quick internal aside, Liam, any gotchas to call out?
[00:25:46] Liam O'Connor: Just that for long sequences and high concurrency you'll want to watch memory pressure and KV cache overhead. Also if you shard by region, watch cross-region synchronization latency.
[00:25:58] Sofia Morales: Noted.
[00:26:20] [00:26:40] Raj Patel: Anything else from Redwood?
[00:26:46] Maya Chen: We'll assemble the bench plan and security pack. Expect Hosted results first.
[00:26:55] [00:27:10] Hannah Liu: We might loop in procurement if numbers look good.
[00:27:15] Maya Chen: Good to know. We'll include a procurement-ready price summary.
[00:27:24] [00:27:40] Eli Turner: One more quick technical: tokenization differences can change tokens/sec — do you normalize on byte-pair tokenizers?
[00:27:48] Priya Rao: Yes, we run tokenization with your tokenizer and report token counts using the same vocab so the numbers are apples-to-apples.
[00:27:56] [00:28:10] Raj Patel: Great. Let's wrap.
[00:28:16] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone; next checkpoint after we share Hosted bench.
[00:28:22] [00:28:36] Meeting ends
